title: 'futhark fmt' does not play well with Literate Futhark

If `futhark fmt` is applied to this program, it significantly changes how it is processed by `futhark literate`: https://github.com/diku-dk/futhark-website/blob/master/examples/3d-vectors.fut

The main problem is that all comments in modules end up being indended to the level of the module.

The solution can either be to adjust `futhark fmt` to not indent comments inside modules, or to modify `futhark literate` to not look only at comments beginning in column zero.

It is very undesirable that these two excellent tools do not work well together.

title: Fix uniqueness violation in diffUpdateAcc for Safe scatter over 2D arrays
body:
## Summary

When applying \`vjp\` to a \`scatter\` over a \`[n][k]f64\` array with a concatenated index array (e.g. \`(0..<n) ++ (0..<n)\`), the compiler crashed with an internal type error after the \`ad\` pass: \`Variable X referenced after being consumed\`.

**Root cause:** In \`diffUpdateAcc\`, the \`Safe\` branch built an \`if\`-expression whose **true branch body** referenced \`adj\` twice in a sequential scope: first observing it via \`Index adj slice\` (to read out \`adj_i\`), then consuming it via \`Update Unsafe adj slice zero\` (to produce \`acc_adj\`). Even though cross-branch consumption is legal in Futhark (it is fine for one branch to consume a variable that the other only observes), within a single branch body the two uses are sequenced, and the type checker fires when a variable is consumed after being observed in the same scope. The bug only triggers for 2D (or higher) element types because those yield \`Safe\` \`UpdateAcc\` statements; 1D scatters use \`Unsafe\` and are unaffected.

**Fix:** Made \`zeroed\` take the array name as a parameter. In the \`Safe\` branch, a copy of \`adj\` (\`adj_copy\`) is made before the \`if\` so the true branch consumes the copy via \`Update Unsafe adj_copy slice zero\` while still observing the original \`adj\` via \`Index adj slice\`. The false branch returns the original \`adj\` unchanged. This eliminates the within-branch conflict entirely.

**Concern:** The copy added in the \`Safe\` branch should be eliminated by simplification in normal cases, but could leave a constant memory overhead if simplification doesn't fire. Also, the \`copyConsumedArrsInStm\` mechanism handles this class of problem for the forward pass generically — generated return-sweep code is not covered by it, so similar issues in other \`diff*\` functions would need their own fixes.

title: Fix dimension naming in register tiling to use x/y/z ordering
body:
`BlkRegTiling.hs` used z/y/x ordering (z=outermost, x=innermost) for dimension names in the generated SegSpace and local variables, while the rest of the codebase (e.g., `TileLoops.hs`) uses x/y/z (x=outermost, z/y=innermost). This made the code inconsistent and harder to reason about.

## Changes

**2D tiling (`mmBlkRegTilingAcc`, `mmBlkRegTilingNrm`)**
- Swap x↔y so `gtid_y`/`gid_y` is now the innermost dimension (consistent with `TileLoops`)
- Generated SegSpace now ends with `(gid_y, gridDim_y)` as the innermost block dim

Before:
```haskell
(gtid_x, width_B) : (gtid_y, height_A) : rem_outer_dims_rev <- reverse $ unSegSpace seg_space
-- space: [(gid_y, gridDim_y), (gid_x, gridDim_x)]   -- x was innermost
```
After:
```haskell
(gtid_y, width_B) : (gtid_x, height_A) : rem_outer_dims_rev <- reverse $ unSegSpace seg_space
-- space: [(gid_x, gridDim_x), (gid_y, gridDim_y)]   -- y is innermost
```

**3D tiling (`doRegTiling3D`)**
- Rename to x=outermost, y=middle, z=innermost of the three inner kernel dims
- `d_M`/`rz`/`tx`/`gid_z` (old outermost) → `d_Kx`/`rx`/`gid_x`
- `d_Kx`/`tx`/`gid_x` (old innermost) → `d_Kz`/`tz`/`gid_z`
- Generated SegSpace now ends with `(gid_z, gridDim_z)` as innermost

Before:
```haskell
(gtid_x, d_Kx) : (gtid_y, d_Ky) : (gtid_z, d_M) : rem_outer_dims_rev
-- x=innermost, z=outermost — z/y/x from outer to inner
```
After:
```haskell
(gtid_z, d_Kz) : (gtid_y, d_Ky) : (gtid_x, d_Kx) : rem_outer_dims_rev
-- z=innermost, x=outermost — x/y/z from outer to inner
```

All downstream variable references (`gridDim_*`, `jj1`/`jj2`/`ii`, thread bindings, bounds checks, `regtile_ret_dims`, `segMap2D`/`segMap3D` call sites) updated accordingly. Pure rename — no semantic changes.

title: GPU code migration produces code with GPU allocation
body:
This fails to compile:

```Futhark
def sa (bellman: [1]f64 -> [1]f64) (V0:[1]f64) (sa_max:i64) (bet:f64) : [1]f64 =
  let sa_min = 2i64
  let sa_tol = 1e-3
  let tol_ratio = 1e-3
  let (res,_,_,_) =
    loop (res, conv, i, tol) = (V0, false, 0i64, 0f64)
      while !conv && i < sa_max do
        let V = bellman res
        let tol' = f64.maximum (map2 (\a b -> f64.abs(a-b)) V res)
        let rtol' = if i == 1 then 1f64 else tol' / tol
        let conv = (i > sa_min && f64.abs(bet - rtol') < tol_ratio)
                || (i > sa_min && tol' < sa_tol)
        in (V, conv, i+1, tol')
  in res

entry main (sa_max: i64) : [1]f64 =
  sa (\x -> [0.5 * (x[0] + 2/x[0])]) [1.4] sa_max 0
```

The reason isn't very interesting; just some allocation that is not hoisted out of a `GPUBody` for some reason. There is a small likelihood we are migrating code to the GPU that we should not, and a larger likelihood that we simply need to hoist more aggressively (since this is a uniform allocation).

title: Support black box primitives
body:
It would be nice if the Futhark IR could have a notion of functions whose semantics are not known to the compiler (or alternatively, where the Futhark representation of them is not intended to be used), and are simply passed through without modification, but can then be handled specially by backends. Cosmin had some students do this through a bit of a hack at one point, but I think we should consider how to handle it more cleanly.

The goal is not immediately [to support a user-visible FFI](https://github.com/diku-dk/futhark/issues/1429) - my immediate use case is for programs that directly produce Futhark IR, and presumably also supply their own backends. Hence we only need to discuss the representation at IR level.

As perhaps the simplest thing, it could be a IR function definition that has the right *type* but a vacuous body, and an attribute indicating that this is just a proxy for an operation that will be slotted in by a backend.

As a slightly more systematic thing, we could extend our definition of a program to also contain a list of "primitives", that would essentially be functions without a body. This would also make it easier to add more bespoke information to these primitives. For example, information about how they use memory. This is not possible by just hacking up normal functions, because it is not possible to talk about memory while the program is in a non-memory IR.

This is of interest to @nhey and perhaps @coancea.

title: Fusion: fuse map-through-flatten into scatter (WithAcc) atomically

labels.name: run-benchmarks
labels.description: Makes GA run the benchmark suite.

body:
## Problem

When a `scatter` is lowered to `with_acc` in the IR, fusion of the pattern

```futhark
let (vals, inds) = unzip (map f xs)
in scatter dest (flatten inds) (flatten vals)
```

stopped working. Before the `with_acc` rewrite, the outer `map` could fuse directly with the scatter. Afterwards, the dependency graph looks like:

```
SoacNode (map f xs)
    ↓ produces [m][n] arrays
TransNode (flatten/reshape)   TransNode (flatten/reshape)
    ↓                              ↓
        StmNode (with_acc)
```

The existing `SoacNode→WithAcc` rule in `vFuseNodeT` requires the two nodes to be *adjacent* in the graph, so it never fires here. The `TransNode→SoacNode` rule cannot help either because the TransNodes feed the WithAcc, not the SoacNode.

## Why the naïve fix causes an infinite loop

The obvious approach — add a `TransNode→WithAcc` rule that moves the reshape inside the lambda — fails with a 100% CPU hang. The simplifier marks `Reshape` as a cheap, safe operation (`safeExp (BasicOp Reshape {}) = True`), so after the reshape is moved inside the WithAcc lambda, `simplifyLambda` immediately hoists it back out. This recreates the same `TransNode` node in the graph, causing `keepTrying` to loop forever.

## Fix

Add `trySoacThroughTransIntoWithAcc`, a graph-level augmentation that absorbs the `SoacNode` and all intermediate `TransNode`s into the `WithAcc` lambda body *atomically* in a single step. Because the SoacNode is now inside the lambda, its 2D outputs are never visible in the outer scope and cannot be hoisted back out. `doFusionInLambda` can then apply `pullReshape` to fuse the map into the inner scatter update.

The rule only commits (increments `fusionCount` to trigger another `keepTrying` iteration) if `doFusionInLambda` actually succeeds, preventing runaway iteration on programs where the pattern matches but inner fusion cannot proceed.

A second required fix is in `commonTransforms'` (`TryFusion.hs`): the two `flatten` calls in the example produce `Reshape` transforms with the same shape but different certificates (each carries the certificate of the branch that produced it). The original `ot1 == ot2` check failed on cert mismatch, preventing `pullReshape` from peeling the common reshape. The fix introduces `compatibleTransforms` which merges certs when shapes match.

## Test

`tests/fusion/WithAccs/issue2452.fut` is a minimal regression test. It expects `Screma 1 WithAcc 1` after the standard pipeline — one top-level Screma (the bounds-check loop) and one WithAcc with the map fused inside it.

title: Fix crash when hole with function type is used in syntactic let-binding (#2488)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #2488.

When a hole (`???`) is the body of a let-defined function with at least one syntactic argument (e.g. `let f _ = ???`), and the result is applied to multiple arguments (e.g. `f true false`), the consumption checker crashed with an unhandled `error` call.

**Root cause:** The consumption checker's `checkArgs` and `applyArg` functions pattern-matched exclusively on `Arrow` types. When the body of the local function is a hole, its return type is an unconstrained type variable (e.g. `*t₁`). Applying this result to a second argument caused `checkArgs` to hit its `error` fallback (`checkArgs: *t₁`), and then `applyArg` had the same issue.

title: Fix non-exhaustive pattern detection when wildcards mix with constructors
body:
Fixes #2483.

## Problem

When a match column contains both wildcard patterns and explicit constructors, `incompleteCase` computed `sigma` (the set of explicit constructors) but discarded the default-matrix witnesses without checking sub-patterns of sigma constructors. If sigma happened to cover all constructors, the function returned `[]` — no warning — even when combinations were genuinely unmatched.

## Fix

Add `recurseOnConstrHeads`: when wildcards are present alongside structural constructors (sum, tuple, record), specialise on each unique constructor head and recurse to find unmatched sub-patterns. Wildcard rows are automatically included via `specialise`, so the check is correct. For Sum types with incomplete sigma, missing constructors are still reported via the default matrix as before.

Literal patterns (`ConstrLit`) are excluded from this path since their domain is infinite and enumeration is not possible.

title: Remove the neutral element from Scan SOACs and SegScan kernels
body:
`Scan` becomes a `newtype` over `Lambda rep` only — no more
`scanNeutral`.  Iteration 0 is handled with an **is_first trick**: a
boolean (init `true`, set `false` after one use) guards the scan
operator so that `op(ne, x) = x` is implemented by taking the map
result directly.  The same trick adapts the GPU single-pass / two-pass
SegScan kernels and the multicore SegScan.

The motivation is freedom from a value-level neutral for monoids
where one isn't natural (user-defined operators, non-`Prim` accs,
costly-to-materialise zeros), plus removing one source of plumbing
drift across fusion, AD, ISRWIM, and ImpGen.

## What's in the PR

- **IR**: `Scan` is `newtype Scan rep = Scan (Lambda rep)`; helpers
  recompute sizes from `lambdaReturnType`.  `SegScanOp` adapted.
- **Lowerings**: `FirstOrderTransform`, `soacToStream`, `ISRWIM`,
  `ExtractKernels`, `ExtractMulticore`, `DistributeNests` no longer
  thread a neutral.  `soacToStream`'s scanomap branch emits a
  per-chunk scanomap as a `Screma` SOAC plus a top-level shift map
  combining the chunk's last value with the cross-chunk accumulator;
  this preserves the baseline path through which
  `ExtractMulticore`/`ExtractKernels` recover an inner `SegScan` from
  scan-into-stream patterns such as `reduce (+) 0 (scan (+) 0 xs)`.
- **Backends**: `ImpGen/GPU/SegScan/{SinglePass,TwoPass}` and
  `ImpGen/Multicore/SegScan` reworked to the no-neutral kernel
  shapes.
- **AD**: `AD/Rev/Scan` builds adjoint scans neutral-free; `AD/Fwd`
  and the other `AD/Rev/*` modules updated mechanically.
- **AD fix**: `AD/Rev/Loop.revLoop` filters loop params whose body
  result is a `Constant` so the adjoint loop's body and merge stay
  in lock-step.  Without this, VJP scan fusion produces a malformed
  adjoint Loop (the precise failure mode of `tests/ad/issue2256.fut`).
- **Simplify**: a new `peelIsFirstParam` rule recognises the
  is_first shape (bool merge param, init `true`, body result
  `Constant False`, used only as the sole scrutinee of top-level
  `Match`es) and peels iteration 0, dropping the merge slot.
  Registered only in the per-backend rule books (`GPU`, `MC`, `Seq`,
  `Mem`), not in `standardRules`.

## Performance

Measured on a GTX 1660 Ti vs. baseline `f2a60a6aa`.  GPU performance
is broadly preserved or improved:

| Pattern                                              | Effect on HEAD |
|------------------------------------------------------|----------------|
| `scan (+) 0f32 xs` at 67 M                           | ~17% faster    |
| `map (scan ...) xs` (rows / cols), various shapes    | 8–18% faster   |
| Generic `scan` on i32/i64/f64/tuples/scanomap        | within noise   |
| Segmented scan, 67 M, short and long segments        | **~7% slower** |

The segmented dip is the only measured runtime regression.

## Downsides

1. **`soacToStream` introduces an in-loop `if`.**  The new scanomap
   stream body wraps the per-chunk scanomap with an
   `if is_first then chunk_scan else map (\x -> scan_lam(acc, x))
   chunk_scan` shift and an analogous `if`-guarded cross-chunk acc
   update.  Both ifs sit at the top level of the body, around the
   inner SOAC, not inside any inner loop.  Two consequences:

   - It triggered the AD `revLoop` mis-shaping bug (fixed here; see
     above).  Reverting the fix breaks VJP scan fusion.
   - Cleaning up the residual `is_first`-shaped loops relies on
     `peelIsFirstParam` in the per-backend simplify.  Any future
     pass that interposes before the simplify will see the un-peeled
     shape.

   In the `sequentialStreamWholeArray` path (which both `ExtractMulticore`
   and `ExtractKernels` use), `is_first` becomes the constant `true`,
   the shift collapses to identity, and the inner per-chunk scanomap
   reduces to a single full-width `Screma` — extracted as a
   `SegScan` by the multicore / GPU walker.

2. **Segmented SegScan ~7% slower on GPU.**  Root cause: the
   no-neutral kernel guards `blockScan` with a runtime-variable
   `valid_threads_cnt` instead of the constant `tblock_size`; NVRTC
   cannot constant-fold this, register pressure rises and per-SM
   occupancy drops.  Restoring parity requires reshaping the
   partial-last-block handling so the check is elided on the common
   path.  Not done here.

3. **`peelIsFirstParam` is conservative.**  Fires only on
   constant-bound loops (≥ 1) and only when the bool param is used
   solely as a top-level `Match` scrutinee.  Symbolic-bound loops,
   nested matches, alias chains, multi-scrutinee matches, and bool
   flowing into nested loops all cause the rule to skip.  AD
   correctness does not depend on the rule firing.

## AD correctness: `eBlank` padding in PPAD reverse-mode scan

`asLiftPPAD` pads `as_lift[n-1]` with `eBlank` (zero/default) rather
than the scan neutral element, and `ysRightPPAD` does the same for
`ys_right[0]`.  Investigation confirmed this does **not** cause
incorrect results:

- The `a3 = op(pa1, pa2)` chain in the lifted reversed scan carries
  the corrupted value, but `diffScan` discards it — only chunk index 2
  (`z`, the actual gradient values) is extracted via `(!! 2) . chunk d`.
  Chunk 1 (`a3`) is dead computation.
- `ys_right[0] = eBlank` is guarded by an explicit `i=0` branch in
  `finalMapPPAD` that returns `r_adj[0]` directly, bypassing the
  operator.

Verified with an assert-based probe (`assert (b1 != 0)` in the
operator, neutral `(0,1)`, `eBlank = (0,0)`) for `n = 2, 3, 4`, with
`simplifyLambda` disabled in `Pass/AD.hs` to prevent constant
propagation from masking the issue.  No assert fired and results were
bit-identical to the reference binary.

```futhark
  match (a,b)

    assert (s == false) (#F(((false, x / b, 1, 1 / b))))
  case (#M, #I(s,x,b)) ->
    assert (s == false) (#I(true,x,b))
  case (#M, #F(s,x,b,f)) ->
    assert (s == false) (#F(true,x,b,f))
  case (#F _, #P) -> assert false (([])[0])
```

title: Invalid memory access for HIP backend
body:
This contrived program does something naughty on at least the HIP backend, but since code generation for this is the same across all GPU backends, it probably affects them all:

```Futhark

-- ==
-- compiled random input { [50][10][30]f32 [50][10][50][30]f32 } auto output

def main [n] [k] [l] (xs: [n][l][k]f32) (ys: [n][l][n][k]f32) =
```

title: Invalid result for terrible reduction operator when using GPU backends
body:
```Futhark
-- ==
-- random input { [10][20][8]i32 [10][20]i32 } auto output

entry main [k] [n] [m] (xss: [k][n][m]i32) (xs: [k][n]i32) =
  map (reduce (\(as0, b0) (as1, b1) -> (map2 (+) as0 as1, b0 + b1)) (replicate m 0, 0))
      (map2 zip xss xs)
  |> unzip
```

This produces the wrong result when using a GPU backend. I suspect it is related to the memory annotations we put on the binary operators in such cases. We never came up with a good design. The function `generalSegRedInterms` has a suggestive comment:

```
          -- This 'segmented' thing here is a hack, related to #2227.
          -- There absolutely must be some unifying principle we are
          -- missing.
```

And indeed, the related control flow is used to avoid constructing a meaningful index function for a temporary array, and instead just hoping that a new one will work:

```
          if segmented
            then ixfun
            else LMAD.iota (tblock_id * product shape_E) shape_E
```

I am quite sure that this is the root of the bug. I am also reasonably confident that this is the cause of #2476.

title: Support Sparse adjoints in vectorised AD
body:
Vectorised AD was forcing `AdjSparse` → `AdjVal` materialisation in `updateAdjIndex` whenever `adj_shape /= mempty`, killing the sparse map optimisation in `vjpMap` that avoids generating a reverse-sweep `Map` when only a constant number of adjoints are nonzero.

The fix: let `Sparse` carry its vector dimension count so the index is applied uniformly across vector elements rather than requiring eager materialisation.

### Changes

- **`Sparse` type**: Added `sparseVecDims :: Int` — number of leading vector dimensions. Zero in the non-vectorised case.
- **`sparseArray`**: Slice now emits full-range dims for vector prefix before `DimFix i`:
  ```haskell
  vec_slice = map sliceDim $ take vec_dims $ shapeDims shape
  -- Update s arr (fullSlice arr_t (vec_slice ++ [DimFix i])) se
  ```
- **`updateAdjIndex`**: Removed `adj_shape == mempty` guards. Always creates `AdjSparse` with shape `adj_shape <> arrayShape t` and the corresponding `vec_dims`.
- **`adjRep`**: Threads `sparseVecDims` through representation round-trip.
- **`vjpMap` `isSparse`**: Matches on array dims only: `drop vd (shapeDims shape) == [w]`.

title: Custom derivatives for reverse-mode.
body:
This morning I realised that it would actually be quite easy to support custom derivatives for reverse mode (and possibly for forward mode, although it's less important). The idea is basically to provide a way for users to specify a different "VJP" operation for some fragment of code, which the AD transform will then just insert.

The user interface is this new intrinsic function:

```Futhark
-- | Provide custom reverse-mode adjoint code for a given function. This is
-- useful when the adjoint synthesised by AD is as good as one that is known
-- analytically.
--
-- The function `f` returns a result of type `b`. In the return sweep, the
-- function `f'` is invoked first with the result of `f` and second with the
-- cotangents of the result (be careful not to mix up the order), and must
-- return the sensitivity with respect to the input.
--
-- A common pattern is that `b` is a tuple where some part is the intended
-- primal result of `vjp_by`, and some part is only used in `f'`.
--
-- **Beware:** if `f` uses any free variables, these will not be taken into
-- **account when computing the adjoint. Make these part of the argument
-- **instead.
def vjp_by 'a 'b 'c (f: a -> b) (f': (res: b) -> (b_adj: b) -> a) (x: a) : b =
  intrinsics.vjp_by f f' x
```

I have written all of one test, but it seems to work quite well. I have not pondered whether this interacts with nested AD in any interesting way. The interpreter just ignores any use of `vjp_by`.

title: Fix loop result alias inference for mixed-diet tuple merge parameters
body:
`checkLoop` could infer incorrect aliases when a loop merge parameter grouped consumed and non-consumed values in a tuple/record. In that shape, alias inference treated the entire merge parameter as consumed, which incorrectly stripped aliases from non-consumed components (e.g. returning `ps` as unique/non-aliased).

- **Alias inference for loop merge arguments**
  - Replaced the synthetic single-parameter function/application path in `checkLoop` with loop-specific alias propagation.
  - Added `applyLoopArg`, which recursively traverses structured merge parameters and applies `returnType` with **per-component** diet (`Consume`/`Observe`) instead of a tuple-wide diet.
  - Kept existing result combination behavior (`combineAliases ... body_als`) unchanged.
  - Simplified the record case in `applyLoopArg` by removing redundant field-set checks and using a shorter `Scalar . Record` style.

- **Regression coverage**
  - Added `tests/loops/loop-aliases0.fut` with the minimal reproducer:
    - merge tuple contains both `cache: *[5]f32` and `ps: [10]f32`
    - loop returns `(cache, ps)`
    - verifies `ps` aliases are preserved through loop result inference.

```futhark
entry main (cache: *[5]f32) (ps: [10]f32) =
  loop (cache: *[5]f32, ps: [10]f32) = (cache, ps)
  for i < 5 do
    (cache, ps)
```

title: Incorrect alias inference for loops
body:
Surprisingly, this simple program is not alias-checked properly:

```Futhark
entry main (cache: *[5]f32) (ps: [10]f32) =
  loop (cache: *[5]f32, ps: [10]f32) = (cache, ps)
  for i < 5 do
    (cache, ps)
```

If passed to `futhark dev`, the compiler will with an IR type checking error, because the frontend type checker has inferred wrong aliases. Specifically, it infers this type for `main`:

```
(cache: *[5]f32) -> (ps: [10]f32) -> (*[5]f32, *[10]f32)
```

Clearly wrong, as the second element of the result tuple clearly aliases the `ps` parameter.

The reason this goes wrong is due to how we generate aliase for loops in the `checkLoop` function. Basically, the way it works is that we synthesize a function type corresponding to the loop, then use the normal aliases-of-function-result logic (`applyArg`) to determine the aliases in the result based on the aliases of the initial loop arguments (`arg_als`). But loops like this don't actually correspond to a Futhark function! The loop above has a single parameter with a consuming part (`cache`) and a nonconsuming part (`ps`). Intuitively, we could imagine this corresponds to this function:

```
(*[5]f32, [10]f32) -> (*[5]f32, [10]f32)
```

But this is not actually a Futhark type, as diet (whether a parameter is consumed) applies to *entire parameters*, not to parts of tuple. This is how it should be and simplified many things, so we will not change this part of the design. But the problem is that we end up constructing this function type for the loop:

```
*([5]f32, [10]f32) -> (*[5]f32, [10]f32)
```

That is, the *entire* loop parameter tuple is treated as consumed (for alias inference purposes only), and by our aliasing rules, that means no part of the result aliases any part of the input.

I believe the solution is to rework the part of `checkLoop` that infers these aliases such that it no longer works by piggybacking directly on the normal function application machinery. Two options seem viable:

1. Continue using the same machinery, but construct a function of *multiple parameters* in those cases where the loop pattern is a syntactic tuple, e.g in the above case we would have: `*[5]f53 -> [10]f32 -> (*[5]f32, [10]f32)`. This would then require multiple applications of `applyArg` to specially constructed argument types corresponding to the initial loop argument.
2. Don't use `applyArg` at all; use a bespoke function that recursively traverses loop parameter type with fine-grained consumption information (`param_t` in the current code) and `arg_als` at the same time. Hopefully the logic in `returnType` can still be reused.

title: Preserve explicit uniqueness for local function returns in consumption checking
body:
The type checker incorrectly rejected some programs with local functions by mis-tracking return alias/uniqueness in loops, even when the local function had an explicit unique return type. This caused valid code to fail unless the helper function was moved to top level.

- **Consumption checker: local function/lambda return handling**
  - In `Language/Futhark/TypeChecker/Consumption.hs`, local `let`-functions and lambdas now preserve explicitly annotated return uniqueness (`te`) instead of always re-inferring uniqueness from body aliases.
  - Uniqueness inference is still used when no explicit return annotation is present.

- **Regression coverage**
  - Added `tests/issue2456.fut` with the reported pattern: a local function returning `(*Cache [dh], Params)` used inside a loop.

- **Behavioral impact**
  - Aligns local function behavior with top-level function behavior for explicit return annotations.
  - Prevents spurious loop alias errors in cases like:

```futhark
let gen_token [dh] (cache: *Cache [dh]) (ps: Params): (*Cache [dh], Params) =
  (cache, ps)
in loop (cache: *Cache [dh], ps: Params) = (cache, ps)
   for i < 5 do
     gen_token cache ps
```

title: Loosen consuming-argument self-alias checks by tracking alias field paths
body:
The consumption checker treated record/tuple aliases too coarsely (variable-level only), so valid consuming calls like `f x` were rejected when `x` was a unique tuple/record value. We now keep field-path information in aliases for overlap detection, while preserving variable-level consumption behavior.

- **Alias model: add field-path precision**
  - Extended `Alias` with `aliasFields` in addition to `aliasVar`.
  - Kept existing bound/free alias distinction, now with path-aware identity.

- **Self-alias detection: only overlap on same var + same field path**
  - Updated self-alias seeding in pattern/parameter/identifier binding to insert aliases per field path.
  - This makes tuple/record components distinct for `noSelfAliases`, avoiding false positives from coarse `{x}` vs `{x}` overlap.

- **Consumption semantics: still variable-level**
  - Consumption checks continue to consume/validate by `aliasVar`.
  - Adjusted consumption alias aggregation to preserve prior “consume the whole record argument” behavior for consuming parameters.

- **Return alias handling updates**
  - Propagated richer alias sets through `checkReturnAlias`, converting to variable sets only where required (e.g. parameter-consumability checks), so return checks remain sound with path-aware aliases.

- **Regression coverage**
  - Added accept case for consuming a unique tuple variable directly.
  - Added reject case to keep rejecting true self-aliasing (`f (x, x)`).

```futhark

def g [n] (x: *([n]i32, [n]i32)) = f x      -- now accepted

def h [n] (x: *[n]i32) = f (x, x)           -- still rejected
```

title: Loosen some of the alias checking for consumption
body:
In the source language, all of our checking related to uniqueness is defined in `Language.Futhark.TypeChecker.Consumption`. The checks are very conservative, and in some cases they make it hopelessly awkward to write code. For example, consider this program:

```Futhark
def f [n] (x: *([n]i32, [n]i32)) = x with 0[0] = 0

def g [n] (x: *([n]i32, [n]i32)) = f x
```

The application `f x` fails to type-check because `x` is "self-aliased". The motivation fine on its own: in the function `f`, we must certainly be free to assume that the components of the tuple do not alias each other, as otherwise consuming one would also consume the other. The intent is to rule out applications like this, which *are* bad:

```Futhark
def h [n] (x: *[n]i32) = f (x, x)
```

Returning to `g`, when we type-check the application `f x`, we check that the argument `x` is not "self-aliased". In our type system, tuples (or records, which is what they really are) do not have any identity, hence aliases are associated only with their fields. This is as intended: constructing tuples should not require us to copy their components. A record is self-aliased whenever any of its fields contain overlapping aliases. The problem is that we only track aliases at the level of *variable names* (and out-of-scope variables, but that doesn't matter here). Hence, in `g`, we could see the aliases of `x` as having the form `({x}, {x})`, meaning it is a tuple where each component has the alias set `{x}`. Clearly they overlap! But this is an overapproximation: each of those fields only aliases *itself*, and if we could track that fact, we could make our self-alias-checking more precise.

I am not interested in tracking *consumption* at an overall level more precisely. If you consume a field of a tuple, I am still fine with treating the entire tuple as consumed. The goal is merely to make it easier to pass around entire records (or tuples) in a consuming way.

I think the solution is to extend the `Alias` definition in `Language.Futhark.TypeChecker.Consumption` such that it can also track a field of a variable, perhaps like so:

```Haskell
data Alias
  = AliasBound {aliasVar :: VName, aliasFields :: [Name]}
  | AliasFree {aliasVar :: VName, aliasFields :: [Name]}
  deriving (Eq, Ord, Show)
```

Then the self-aliasing check (in e.g. `noSelfAliases`) considers alias sets to only overlap if they contain the same variable *and* the same fields. In all other cases where we consume something through an alias, we still consider only the `aliasVar`.

I think it is not too difficult to implement. Consumption is fairly cleanly factored into its own module (although it would be nice to formalise it at some point...). Apart from the above sketched changes, we would also need to change `bindingPat` (which is where aliases are inserted into bound variables, as every variable `x` is initially marked as aliasing `x`). Probably `checkReturnAlias` would also need to be modified.

title: Unify C server array metadata and callback types into a single `struct array`
body:
The C server runtime had split array metadata across `array` and `array_aux`, plus parallel callback type families (`array_*` vs `aux_array_*`). This change consolidates array representation and callback typing to eliminate duplication and reduce cross-structure drift risk.

- **Runtime type model consolidation (`rts/c/server.h`)**
  - Removed `struct array_aux`.
  - Expanded `struct array` to carry all array metadata and operations previously split across both structs (`rank`, element type, primitive info/name, zip field metadata, and all callbacks).
  - Replaced `aux_array_*` typedefs with unified array callback typedefs.

- **Array operation plumbing updates**
  - Updated zip/unzip paths to use `struct array` directly (no `a->aux` indirection).
  - Updated generic array serialization helpers to take `const struct array*`:
    - `restore_array`
    - `store_array`
    - `free_array`
  - Aligned restore/store/free logic with unified callback signatures.

- **Codegen alignment (`src/Futhark/CodeGen/Backends/GenericC/Server.hs`)**
  - Stopped generating separate `array_aux` objects.
  - Emit a single `struct array` initializer for both plain and opaque-array cases.
  - Updated generated callback casts to unified typedefs.
  - Point type `.aux` to the unified array descriptor where array restore/store/free consume that metadata.

```c
const struct array my_type_array = {
  .rank = ...,
  .element_type = ...,
  .info = ...,
  .name = "...",
  .num_fields = ...,
  .fields = ...,
  .new = (array_new_fn)...,
  .set = (array_set_fn)...,
  .shape = (array_shape_fn)...,
  .index = (array_index_fn)...,
  .values = (array_values_fn)...,
  .free = (array_free_data_fn)...,

};
```

title: Fix GPU segmented reduction strategy selection for noncommutative operators
body:
GPU backends could miscompile a noncommutative segmented reduction when `#[incremental_flattening(only_inner)]` is used and commutativity is hidden with `opaque`. The small-vs-large segmented reduction strategy heuristic incorrectly depended on the noncommutative chunk factor.

- **Codegen fix (SegRed strategy selection)**
  - Updated segmented reduction path selection in `src/Futhark/CodeGen/ImpGen/GPU/SegRed.hs` to stop multiplying the small-segment threshold by `chunk`.
  - This avoids routing large-segment noncommutative reductions into the small-segment kernel due to chunking-specific tuning.

- **Regression coverage**
  - Added `tests/issue2450.fut` with the reported reproducer to lock in correct behavior for segmented noncommutative reductions under incremental flattening.

```haskell
-- Before
use_small_segments = segment_size * 2 .<. pe64 (unCount tblock_size) * tvExp chunk_v

-- After
use_small_segments = segment_size * 2 .<. pe64 (unCount tblock_size)
```

title: Miscompilation of non-commutative segmented reduction with GPU backends
body:
This program produces the wrong result when compiled with a GPU backend:

```Futhark
-- ==
-- compiled random input { [1][256]i32 } auto output
-- compiled random input { [100][256]i32 } auto output
-- compiled random input { [100][512]i32 } auto output

def main xs = #[incremental_flattening(only_inner)] map (reduce (\x y -> opaque x + y) 0i32) xs
```

The attribute is to cut down on the code size, and the `opaque` is to prevent the compiler from recognising the operator as commutative.

It is a strange bug, because noncommutative reductions certainly work in general - *unless* it just so happens that we don't have a single test case for *segmented* commutative reductions.

title: Monomorphise: propagate size-arg lift info through let-bindings
body:
When a polymorphic function `f` is monomorphised into `f_mono` with extra explicit size parameters, that lift info was stored in `sLifts` under `f` but never propagated to names bound via `let h = f`. Consequently, `h a b g` took the fallback Apply path and omitted the required size argument.

```futhark
def f (n: i64) (m: i64) (g: f64 -> [m ** n]f64) = g 0

entry main a b =
  let h = f          -- h never got f's lift info
  in h a b (\x -> replicate (b ** a) x)  -- missing size arg → failure
```

## Changes

- **`Monomorphise.hs` — `transformAppExp (LetPat ...)`**: after transforming the RHS, if the original RHS is a `Var` pointing to a lifted function, register each pattern-bound name in `sLifts` with the same `(f_mono, infer, num_size_args)` entry. This causes subsequent applications of those names to go through the size-arg–inserting Apply path rather than the fallback, making all occurrences fully saturated.

title: Fix horizontal fusion missed due to duplicate inputs not being eliminated
body:
After horizontal fusion, the combined screma can end up with duplicate entries in its input list when two SOACs share the same input array. Without deduplication, the fused screma looks structurally "heavier" than it should, causing the fusion pass to miss subsequent fusion opportunities in the same iteration.

## Changes

- **`src/Futhark/Optimise/Fusion/Screma.hs`**: Call `dedupInput` at the end of `fuseSuperScrema`, applied to `inp_r` and `lam1` before the `SuperScrema` is returned. This is where duplicates are actually introduced (`inp_r = inp_p <> inp_c_real`), and deduplicating here removes extra lambda parameters by replacing them with let-binding aliases of the canonical parameter.

- **`tests/fusion/horizontal-fusion-shared-input.fut`**: Regression test for the pattern from the issue — two outer maps over a shared array `W`, each computing a dot product against different matrices, followed by an elementwise combination:

```futhark
def dotprod [n] (xs: [n]i32) (ys: [n]i32) : i32 =
  i32.sum (map2 (i32.*) xs ys)

entry main W A WH =
  let W_TA  = map (\Wr -> map (\Ac  -> dotprod Wr Ac)  (transpose A))  W
  let W_TWH = map (\Wr -> map (\WHc -> dotprod Wr WHc) (transpose WH)) W
  let H_update = map2 (map2 (i32./)) W_TA W_TWH
  in H_update
```

Without the fix the total `Screma` count in the SOACS pipeline is 4; with it, the two innermost reductions fuse horizontally and the count drops to 3.

title: Fix 'cleanSource' function, re-add nixpkgs Nix formatter.
body:
## The problem with the current `cleanSource`

Currently the `cleanSource` function grabs any files matching the list of regular expressions. In flakes, these files will be put in a new derivation, with a name based on the NAR info of the flake that has been evaluated.

This means that any changes to anything that is tracked by git, will result in a `src` input with a new name, triggering a full rebuild of anything that uses `./.` as a source, even if all of the files found through the regex are the exact same as the previous derivation with a different name.

To test this, run `nix build`, then change one character in any file tracked by git in the repo, and run `nix build` again.


## The solution

Use the `builtins.path` function to import the path, set a name (I've arbitrarily chodsen `futhark-${commit}-src`), and use the regex from the old  `cleanSource` in the `filter` attribute. The result is that any changes to anything that does not relate to the actual build will have no impact on the build, and unnecessary rebuilds are avoided.

The code added is lifted from the [nixpkgs lib][lib], and edited to match the existing `cleanSource` function. Therefore it should be super robust, and unlikely to ever break.

[lib]: https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/1c3fe55ad329cbcb28471bb30f05c9827f724c76/lib/sources.nix#L215

I have built every package in the repo, and everything builds successfully, works, and it resilient to being needlessly rebuilt on arbitrary changes.

## Other changes

I have re-added the nixpkgs Nix formatter as `formatter` in the flake output. It only takes up one line of code, and will be immensely useful for making changes to the Nix code in the future.

title: Fix crash in TileLoops when redomap input array is also used in postlude
body:
`mmBlkRegTiling` produces invalid IR when a SegMap contains two redomaps sharing an input array — the first redomap is tiled (its input slice goes into `tab_inv_stm` for shared-memory loading), but the second redomap in the postlude still references that same slice variable, which no longer exists in the epilogue's scope.

## Changes

- **`src/Futhark/Optimise/BlkRegTiling.hs`** — Added a guard in `matchesBlkRegTile` that returns `Nothing` if any key in `tab_inv_stm` (tiled redomap inputs) is also free in the postlude code (`code2'' <> code2`). This causes `mmBlkRegTiling` to decline and fall through to `tileInKernelBody`, which handles the case correctly by placing invariant prelude definitions in the outer kernel body where they remain in scope.

- **`tests/tiling/issue2467.fut`** — Regression test using a matrix multiply + entrywise divide pattern that triggers the two-redomap-sharing-an-input scenario:

```futhark
entry main W A WH =
  let W_TA  = matmul (transpose W) A
  let W_TWH = matmul (transpose W) WH
  in matdiv_entrywise W_TA W_TWH
```

title: Compiler crash after tiling
body:
The following program makes the TileLoops pass in `src/Futhark/Optimise/TileLoops.hs` produce invalid IR, with a reference to an unknown variable:

```Futhark
def dotprod [n] (xs: [n]i32) (ys: [n]i32) : i32 =
  #[sequential] i32.sum (map2 (i32.*) xs ys)

def matmul [n] [p] [m] (xss: [n][p]i32) (yss: [p][m]i32) : *[n][m]i32 =
  map (\xs -> map (dotprod xs) (transpose yss)) xss

def matdiv_entrywise [m] [n] (xss: [m][n]i32) (yss: [m][n]i32) : *[m][n]i32 =
  map2 (map2 (i32./)) xss yss

entry main W A WH =
  let W_TA = matmul (transpose W) A
  let W_TWH = matmul (transpose W) WH
  let H_update = matdiv_entrywise W_TA W_TWH
  in H_update
```

The `#[sequential]` attribute is just to cut down on code size due to multi-versioning; it is irrelevant to the bug. It is reproduced like so:

```
      let {as_transformed_row_6769 : [n₆_6242]i32} =

      let {as_transformed_row_6770 : [n₆_6242]i32} =
        transpose_res_6471[gtid_6766, 0i64 :+ n₆_6242 * 1i64]
      "test2.fut:11:14-36->test2.fut:5:20-27->test2.fut:2:17-44"
      let {defunc_res_6771 : i32} =
        #[sequential]
        redomap(n₆_6242,
                {as_transformed_row_6768, as_transformed_row_6769},
                \ {eta_p_6772 : i32,

                  : {i32} ->

                  let {*_res_6774 : i32} =

                  in {*_res_6774},
                {\ {eta_p_6775 : i32,
                    eta_p_6776 : i32}
                  : {i32} ->
                  "test2.fut:11:14-36->test2.fut:5:20-27->test2.fut:2:17-44"
                  let {+_res_6777 : i32} =
                    add32(eta_p_6775, eta_p_6776)
                  in {+_res_6777},

      "test2.fut:12:15-38->test2.fut:5:20-27->test2.fut:2:17-44"
      let {defunc_res_6778 : i32} =
        #[sequential]
        redomap(n₆_6242,
                {as_transformed_row_6768, as_transformed_row_6770},
                \ {eta_p_6779 : i32,
                   eta_p_6780 : i32}
                  : {i32} ->
                  "test2.fut:12:15-38->test2.fut:5:20-27->test2.fut:2:31-38"
                  let {*_res_6781 : i32} =
                    mul32(eta_p_6779, eta_p_6780)
                  in {*_res_6781},
                {\ {eta_p_6782 : i32,
                    eta_p_6783 : i32}
                  : {i32} ->
                  "test2.fut:12:15-38->test2.fut:5:20-27->test2.fut:2:17-44"
                  let {+_res_6784 : i32} =
                    add32(eta_p_6782, eta_p_6783)
                  in {+_res_6784},
                {0i32}},
                nilFn)
```

This is in principle correct behaviour from kernel extraction. However, at this point `as_transformed_row_6768` does not exist.

There are several possible options:

1. Introduce support for tiling *multiple* loops at the same time, in the same kernel, as long as they have the same size.
2. Do not tile a loop if its input array is used in the postlude.
3. Make input arrays available in the postlude under their original names. Since the postlude can access (reconstructed forms of) the original kernel space IDs, this should be perfectly possible.

In the future we might also want to rethink how we do kernel extraction on code like this, because it really would have been better to carve this `SegMap` in two, but that is for a different time. Loop tiling should not produce invalid code, no matter how dubious the input.

title: Move Nix pinning system from 'niv' to flakes, spring cleaning in Nix code.
body:
## Why move to flakes

Despite still being labeled experimental, flakes have become the de facto pinning system that almost everyone in the Nix ecosystem uses. They come with benefits other than pinning, like the new `nix` command CLI, truly reproducible and deterministic builds with restricted evaluation.

The flake in this PR is introduced as a superset of the original behaviour. Merging this would allow flake and non-flake users to interact with the Nix in this codebase in the way they prefer. 

With these changes the command `niv update nixpkgs -b master` is superseded by `nix flake update`.


## How does this affect non-flake users

No changes in workflow are needed for non-flake users. This includes the GitHub CI, which I have tested and found to work just fine. These changes would roll out without non-flake users noticing anything had changed.


## What changes have been made

### 1. Move pinning system from `niv` to Nix flakes

Implemented by having the `nix/sources.nix` file read the `flake.lock` file using `flake-compat`, and returning the flake inputs. In essence the old `sources.nix` and `sources.json` are replaced by the new `sources.nix` and `flake.lock`.

The result of this is that `import ./nix/sources.nix` keeps the same behaviour as with the `niv` setup. 

The `flake.nix` that flake users interact with is very simple, and basically sets up the devshells, formatter, and a couple of packages for all flake exposed systems.

Last, the nixpkgs version in the `flake.lock` file is the same as the current one `niv` setup is pinned to.


### 2. Format code with official nixpkgs formatter

Have all Nix code follow the same, modern formatting conventions. In the future this formatter can be run with `nix fmt`.


### 3. Update some expressions to modern conventions

Shells defined with `pkgs.stdenv.mkDerivation { buildInputs = [ ... ]; }` become `pkgs.mkShell { packages = [ ... ]; }`, remove all uses of `rec`, introduction of flakes, modern formatting, etc.


### 4. Split futhark release-tarball derivation creation up into clear separate steps

The current definition of the tarball made by running `nix-build` is a mouthful. I have split it up into three steps in the new `default.nix`. First, the base `futhark` derivation is defined, then the `futhark-static` derivation overrides the first by making the build static, then the tarball derivation is defined, taking the `futhark-static` derivation in as an input.

All three derivations are available as packages in `flake.nix`, with the default one being the tarball. Running `nix-build` still results in the tarball being built.

Splitting things up like this should make it much easier to maintain, and comprehend how the whole thing fits together.


### 5. Remove unused file (nix/zlib.nix)

In the spirit of cleaning up the Nix code, I have removed this file as it isn't referred to anywhere in the codebase.

title: Code Shrinker
body: It would be great if Futhark had a tool like [C-Reduce](https://github.com/csmith-project/creduce), where the tool tries to shrink a program as much as possible while having it still fulfill a property. I am specifically interested in the ability to find a minimal programs which still produce an internal compiler error.
